metadata.title: IQ Test Practice and Review: A Four-Week Schedule
metadata.description: Use an original rule example, counterexamples, error logs, and an adjustable four-week schedule to review strategies in new materials and learning tasks.

faq_items.question: Can Four Weeks of Training Raise IQ?
faq_items.answer: This four-week schedule has not been validated for effectiveness and does not guarantee an IQ increase. You can record strategy use, specific errors, and performance on similar new items, but those personal observations do not by themselves establish transfer, a training cause, or increased overall intelligence.

faq_items.question: How Long Should I Practice Each Day?
faq_items.answer: Use small amounts that do not noticeably affect study, work, or rest. A fixed frequency and high-quality reviews are usually easier to observe than large amounts of practice in one session.

faq_items.question: Should I Repeat the Same Test?
faq_items.answer: Using the same question bank to demonstrate improvement is not recommended because memory and familiarity effects interfere with judgments. Use lawfully obtained, permitted practice with similar but unused materials, and record conditions and reasoning. Better performance on new materials still does not establish transfer or increased intelligence from a personal before-and-after comparison alone.

faq_items.question: If My Score Does Not Improve, Has Training Failed?
faq_items.answer: Not necessarily. First examine error types, strategy execution, and consistency. If these also do not improve, adjust strategies or stop rather than blaming yourself.

faq_items.question: Can Children or Students Follow This Training?
faq_items.answer: This article presents general learning strategies, not an educational or clinical program. Guardians and appropriate education professionals should choose tools for minors based on actual needs. Online results must not be used to label children's ability.
